In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: MolEdit: Knowledge Editing for Multimodal Molecule Language Models
papers.research_question: How to edit knowledge in multimodal molecule language models (MoLMs) to correct inaccuracies while preserving unrelated knowledge, specifically for molecule-to-caption and caption-to-molecule generation tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MolEdit, a framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, and MEBench, a benchmark for evaluating such editing, addressing molecule-specific challenges of multifaceted expertise and cross-molecule interdependence.
papers.conclusion: MolEdit provides an effective framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, enabling precise knowledge updates while preserving unrelated information, and MEBench offers a comprehensive evaluation benchmark, charting a path toward safer, continuously updatable scientific foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
MolEdit outperforms fine-tuning, gradient-based (MEND), and memory-based (GRACE) baselines across Reliability, Locality, and Generality metrics on both MoMu and MolFM backbones.
MolEdit achieves up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than state-of-the-art editing baselines.
Editing molecule generation is more challenging than editing caption generation, and performance is generally better on MoMu than on MolFM.
The Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter (MEKA) effectively routes different facets of molecular knowledge to specialized experts, and the Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher (EAES) accurately activates edits only for relevant inputs.
Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component (MEKA and EAES) to MolEdit's overall performance.
papers.limitation:
Editing molecular SMILES strings is inherently more complex and abstract than editing captions, lacking explicit semantic structure.
Potential misuse of editing to amplify unsafe molecular knowledge and inadvertent propagation of dataset biases.
future_direction: Future work on editing MoLMs.
papers.abstract: Understanding and continuously refining multimodal molecular knowledge is crucial for advancing biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science. Molecule language models (MoLMs) have become powerful tools in these domains, integrating structural representations (e.g., SMILES strings, molecular graphs) with rich contextual descriptions (e.g., physicochemical properties). However, MoLMs can encode and propagate inaccuracies due to outdated web-mined training corpora or malicious manipulation, jeopardizing downstream discovery pipelines. While knowledge editing has been explored for general-domain AI, its application to MoLMs remains uncharted, presenting unique challenges due to the multifaceted and interdependent nature of molecular knowledge. In this paper, we take the first step toward MoLM editing for two critical tasks: molecule-to-caption generation and caption-to-molecule generation. To address molecule-specific challenges, we propose MolEdit, a powerful framework that enables targeted modifications while preserving unrelated molecular knowledge. MolEdit combines a Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter that routes edits to specialized experts for different molecular facets with an Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher that activates the adapters only when input closely matches the stored edits across all expertise, minimizing interference with unrelated knowledge. To systematically evaluate editing performance, we introduce MEBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing multiple dimensions, including Reliability (accuracy of the editing), Locality (preservation of irrelevant knowledge), and Generality (robustness to reformed queries). Across extensive experiments on two popular MoLM backbones, MolEdit delivers up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than baselines while maintaining efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/LzyFischer/MolEdit.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: LAVA: Explainability for Unsupervised Latent Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we explain the organization of latent embeddings from unsupervised models by relating input features to the structure of the embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LA V A, a post-hoc model-agnostic method that explains unsupervised latent embeddings by extracting modules of feature covariation that reoccur across local neighborhoods in the embedding space.
papers.conclusion: LA V A offers a stable and effective approach for explaining unsupervised latent embeddings, revealing interpretable patterns of feature covariation that are missed by existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
LA V A provides stable explanations across different locality placements and module extraction runs.
LA V A modules capture globally reoccurring local subpatterns of feature correlation, not averaged patterns.
The method reveals domain-relevant patterns, such as visual parts in MNIST and disease-related gene expression in kidney cells.
LA V A outperforms the label-free explainability framework in capturing meaningful local structure.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised black-box models are drivers of scientific discovery, yet are difficult to interpret, as their output is often a multidimensional embedding rather than a well-defined target. While explainability for supervised learning uncovers how input features contribute to predictions, its unsupervised counterpart should relate input features to the structure of the learned embeddings. However, adaptations of supervised model explainability for unsupervised learning provide either single-sample or dataset-summary explanations, remaining too fine-grained or reductive to be meaningful, and cannot explain embeddings without mapping functions. To bridge this gap, we propose LAVA, a post-hoc model-agnostic method to explain local embedding organization through feature covariation in the original input data. LAVA explanations comprise modules, capturing local subpatterns of input feature correlation that reoccur globally across the embeddings. LAVA delivers stable explanations at a desired level of granularity, revealing domain-relevant patterns such as visual parts of images or disease signals in cellular processes, otherwise missed by existing methods.

papers.title: Multi-scale Graph Autoregressive Modeling: Molecular Property Prediction via Next Token Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the gap between graph topology preservation and scalable autoregressive training to enable decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CamS bridges the gap between graph topology and autoregressive training, enabling effective molecular property prediction via next-token prediction with a standard decoder-only Transformer backbone.
papers.key_findings:
CamS-LLaMA achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and MoleculeACE benchmarks.
Multi-scale concatenation is the key driver of performance.
The causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining structural differences.
CamS provides a more nuanced structural discrimination than descriptor-based approaches like KPGT.
The method combines general-purpose robustness with fine-grained structural discriminability.
papers.limitation: Vocabulary materialization involves expensive subgraph-isomorphism matching that prohibits direct training on billion-scale corpora.
papers.abstract: We present Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via standard next-token prediction (NTP). For molecular property prediction, SMILES-based NTP scales well but lacks explicit topology, whereas graph-native masked modeling captures connectivity but risks disrupting the pivotal chemical details (e.g., activity cliffs). CamS bridges this gap by serializing molecular graphs into structure-rich causal sequences. CamS first mines data-driven connection-aware motifs. It then serializes motifs via scaffold-rooted breadth-first search (BFS) to establish a stable core-to-periphery order. Crucially, CamS enables hierarchical modeling by concatenating sequences from fine to coarse motif scales, allowing the model to condition global scaffolds on dense, uncorrupted local structural evidence. We instantiate CamS-LLaMA by pre-training a vanilla LLaMA backbone on CamS sequences. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and the activity-cliff benchmark MoleculeACE, outperforming both SMILES-based language models and strong graph baselines. Interpretability analysis confirms that our multi-scale causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining differences.

papers.title: Uncertainty in latent representations of variational autoencoders optimized for visual tasks
papers.research_question: How can we improve uncertainty representations in variational autoencoders for visual inference, especially under contrast changes, image corruption, and out-of-distribution detection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Explaining-Away Variational Autoencoder (EA-VAE), which adds a global scaling latent variable to the standard VAE, leading to improved uncertainty representations in visual inference tasks.
papers.conclusion: The EA-VAE is a simple yet powerful update to the VAE architecture that remedies defective inference of uncertainty in probabilistic computations, with broad applicability in computer vision.
papers.key_findings:
EA-VAE produces contrast-dependent posteriors that match normative requirements of probabilistic inference, unlike standard VAE.
EA-VAE improves out-of-distribution detection by assigning higher uncertainty to OOD samples.
EA-VAE shows better uncertainty estimates for corrupted images (e.g., blurring, noise).
EA-VAE promotes disentanglement of latent variables.
EA-VAE's encoder exhibits divisive normalization, a biological neural computation motif.
future_direction: Assess the benefits of EA-VAEs in non-visual modalities.
Explore the role of explaining away variables in other neural architectures.
papers.abstract: Deep Generative Models (DGMs) can learn flexible latent variable representations of images while avoiding intractable computations, common in Bayesian inference. However, investigating the properties of inference in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), a major class of DGMs, reveals severe problems in their uncertainty representations. Here we draw inspiration from classical computer vision to introduce an inductive bias into the VAE by incorporating a global explaining-away latent variable, which remedies defective inference in VAEs. Unlike standard VAEs, the Explaing-Away VAE (EA-VAE) provides uncertainty estimates that align with normative requirements across a wide spectrum of perceptual tasks, including image corruption, interpolation, and out-of-distribution detection. We find that restored inference capabilities are delivered by developing a motif in the inference network (the encoder) which is widespread in biological neural networks: divisive normalization. Our results establish EA-VAEs as reliable tools to perform inference under deep generative models with appropriate estimates of uncertainty.

papers.title: Analyzing the Hidden Activations of Deep Policy Networks: Why Representation Matters
papers.research_question: Is it possible to know a priori if a state representation will lead to fast learning in deep reinforcement learning agents, and how do neural network policies organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-learned latent representations accelerate policy learning by providing an innately organized internal representation, and a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for good policy learning.
papers.conclusion: Learning a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for effective policy learning, and using pre-learned latent representations can remove this burden, leading to accelerated training.
papers.key_findings:
Agents trained on latent representations learn significantly faster than those trained on raw pixel images.
The internal representation of policies using latent codes is organized around task rewards even before training begins.
A poor initial representation (e.g., raw pixels in a complex task) can cause an unrecoverable collapse in the policy network's internal representation.
The organization of the internal representation evolves during training and correlates with learning progress.
The innate organization provided by latent representations is robust to different weight initialization schemes.
papers.abstract: We analyze the hidden activations of neural network policies of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents and show, empirically, that it's possible to know a priori if a state representation will lend itself to fast learning. RL agents in high-dimensional states have two main learning burdens: (1) to learn an action-selection policy and (2) to learn to discern between useful and non-useful information in a given state. By learning a latent representation of these high-dimensional states with an auxiliary model, the latter burden is effectively removed, thereby leading to accelerated training progress. We examine this phenomenon across tasks in the PyBullet Kuka environment, where an agent must learn to control a robotic gripper to pick up an object. Our analysis reveals how neural network policies learn to organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training. The results from this analysis provide three main insights into how deep RL agents learn. First, a well-organized internal representation within the policy network is a prerequisite to learning good action-selection. Second, a poor initial representation can cause an unrecoverable collapse within a policy network. Third, a good initial representation allows an agent's policy network to organize its internal representation even before any training begins.

papers.title: $\textit{Revelio}$: Interpreting and leveraging semantic information in diffusion models
papers.research_question: What flavors of visual information are captured in different layers and timesteps of a diffusion model? How do they interact and complement each other? What inductive biases are captured in convolution-based vs transformer-based diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Revelio, a method using k-sparse autoencoders (k-SAE) to uncover monosemantic interpretable features in diffusion models, and demonstrates the effectiveness of diffusion features for transfer learning via a lightweight classifier (Diff-C).
papers.key_findings:
Representation granularity varies non-linearly with model depth, with different layers capturing varying levels of visual semantics.
Representation granularity and generalizability vary with diffusion architectures, pre-training data, and design choices like latent vs pixel space.
k-sparse autoencoders help isolate monosemantic visual properties across model states, aiding interpretation.
Diffusion features are effective for discriminative tasks and visual reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight classifier.
Different diffusion timesteps capture different information granularities, with earlier timesteps better for fine-grained tasks.
future_direction: Deeper investigation into why additional noise at certain timesteps (e.g., t=200) helps feature generalizability.
Further research to understand why SD 1.5 performs better than SD 2.1 across timesteps, as noted in prior zero-shot classification work.
papers.abstract: We study $\textit{how}$ rich visual semantic information is represented within various layers and denoising timesteps of different diffusion architectures. We uncover monosemantic interpretable features by leveraging k-sparse autoencoders (k-SAE). We substantiate our mechanistic interpretations via transfer learning using light-weight classifiers on off-the-shelf diffusion models' features. On $4$ datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of diffusion features for representation learning. We provide an in-depth analysis of how different diffusion architectures, pre-training datasets, and language model conditioning impacts visual representation granularity, inductive biases, and transfer learning capabilities. Our work is a critical step towards deepening interpretability of black-box diffusion models. Code and visualizations available at: https://github.com/revelio-diffusion/revelio

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Human-interpretable model explainability on high-dimensional data
papers.research_question: How to provide human-interpretable model explanations on high-dimensional data by using semantic latent features and adapting the Shapley framework.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for model explainability on high-dimensional data that encodes raw inputs into semantic latent features and applies Shapley explainability to these features, providing interpretable, theoretically-controlled explanations.
papers.conclusion: The framework offers a principled, flexible way to achieve human-interpretable explainability on complex models and is hoped to be widely applicable.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarially robust classifiers are less sensitive to high-frequency information compared to non-robust models.
Texture classification models depend on high-frequency periodic patterns in images.
Disentangled latent representations can correctly attribute model decisions to known factors of variation (e.g., scale and position in dSprites).
In CelebA, a model predicting attractiveness shows bias towards gender and age, as revealed by semantic explanations.
The framework provides interpretable explanations that are not possible with pixel-based methods.
papers.limitation: The quality of explanations depends on the semantic representation; if the representation is not well-disentangled, explanations may be corrupted.
papers.abstract: The importance of explainability in machine learning continues to grow, as both neural-network architectures and the data they model become increasingly complex. Unique challenges arise when a model's input features become high dimensional: on one hand, principled model-agnostic approaches to explainability become too computationally expensive; on the other, more efficient explainability algorithms lack natural interpretations for general users. In this work, we introduce a framework for human-interpretable explainability on high-dimensional data, consisting of two modules. First, we apply a semantically meaningful latent representation, both to reduce the raw dimensionality of the data, and to ensure its human interpretability. These latent features can be learnt, e.g. explicitly as disentangled representations or implicitly through image-to-image translation, or they can be based on any computable quantities the user chooses. Second, we adapt the Shapley paradigm for model-agnostic explainability to operate on these latent features. This leads to interpretable model explanations that are both theoretically controlled and computationally tractable. We benchmark our approach on synthetic data and demonstrate its effectiveness on several image-classification tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Explainable AI in drug discovery: self-interpretable graph neural network for molecular property prediction using concept whitening
papers.research_question: How can concept whitening be adapted to graph neural networks to create self-interpretable models for molecular property prediction in drug discovery, and does this improve both performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the concept whitening (CW) interpretability method to graph neural networks, enabling self-interpretable QSAR models that align latent space axes with known molecular properties (concepts) and identify relevant structural parts of molecules for predictions.
papers.conclusion: The adaptation of concept whitening to graph neural networks provides an effective framework for building self-interpretable models in drug discovery, offering improved performance and clear insights into the molecular properties driving predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Adding concept whitening layers to GNNs improves classification performance (ROC-AUC) and interpretability on molecular property prediction tasks.
The method successfully identifies which predefined molecular properties (concepts) are most relevant for predictions at different network depths.
Two novel activation modes for CW in GNNs (weighted_topk_pool and topk_pool) are introduced and evaluated.
The choice of normalization layer (BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm) in the base model affects the performance after adding CW layers.
The method provides both structural (via GNNExplainer) and conceptual explanations for model predictions in drug discovery.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: Explaining Representation by Mutual Information
papers.research_question: How can neural network representations be fully explained using mutual information to decompose them into total, decision-related, and redundant information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based framework that decomposes neural network representations into three exhaustive components: total mutual information, decision-related information, and redundant information, providing a holistic interpretation of representation content.
papers.conclusion: The mutual information framework fully explains the input-representation relationship by capturing all encoded content, decision drivers, and discardable noise, establishing a robust tool for representation analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes total information, decision-related information, and redundant information in image classification tasks using ResNet50, offering more comprehensive explanations than Grad-CAM.
In few-shot learning with a prototype network, the heatmaps for total information and decision-related information show clear differences, highlighting distinct aspects of the representation.
papers.abstract: As interpretability gains attention in machine learning, there is a growing need for reliable models that fully explain representation content. We propose a mutual information (MI)-based method that decomposes neural network representations into three exhaustive components: total mutual information, decision-related information, and redundant information. This theoretically complete framework captures the entire input-representation relationship, surpassing partial explanations like those from Grad-CAM. Using two lightweight modules integrated into architectures such as CNNs and Transformers,we estimate these components and demonstrate their interpretive power through visualizations on ResNet and prototype network applied to image classification and few-shot learning tasks. Our approach is distinguished by three key features: 1. Rooted in mutual information theory, it delivers a thorough and theoretically grounded interpretation, surpassing the scope of existing interpretability methods. 2. Unlike conventional methods that focus on explaining decisions, our approach centers on interpreting representations. 3. It seamlessly integrates into pre-existing network architectures, requiring only fine-tuning of the inserted modules.

papers.title: Is This Just Fantasy? Language Model Representations Reflect Human Judgments of Event Plausibility
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable)? How do these representations develop, do they reflect human categorization behavior, and what interpretable features do they correspond to?
papers.core_contribution: Language models form linear representations (modal difference vectors) that distinguish between modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable). These vectors are more diagnostic than output probabilities, emerge in an intuitive order during training, and reflect fine-grained human categorization behavior and interpretable features like event likelihood and imageability.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn internal representations of modal categories that go beyond output probabilities. These representations develop in an intuitive order and capture nuanced aspects of human categorization, offering a novel way to study world models in LMs and potentially human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Modal difference vectors within LM hidden states reliably classify sentences by modal category, outperforming classification based on sentence probability.
Modal difference vectors develop in a consistent order: inconceivable vs. others emerges first, followed by probable vs. impossible, then probable vs. improbable, and finally improbable vs. impossible.
Projections of sentences onto modal difference vectors create a feature space that accurately models human participants' graded categorization judgments.
Projections along the impossible-inconceivable vector correlate selectively with human ratings of imageability and the presence of physical objects/places.
Preliminary steering experiments show that adding modal difference vectors to the residual stream during generation can influence the modal category of the generated text.
future_direction: Using modal difference vectors to test the intuitive theories about the world that LMs encode from text.
Using modal difference vectors to generate hypotheses about human representations of modal categories, such as the role of imagination in distinguishing impossible from inconceivable events.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are used for a diverse range of tasks, from question answering to writing fantastical stories. In order to reliably accomplish these tasks, LMs must be able to discern the modal category of a sentence (i.e., whether it describes something that is possible, impossible, completely nonsensical, etc.). However, recent studies have called into question the ability of LMs to categorize sentences according to modality (Michaelov et al., 2025; Kauf et al., 2023). In this work, we identify linear representations that discriminate between modal categories within a variety of LMs, or modal difference vectors. Analysis of modal difference vectors reveals that LMs have access to more reliable modal categorization judgments than previously reported. Furthermore, we find that modal difference vectors emerge in a consistent order as models become more competent (i.e., through training steps, layers, and parameter count). Notably, we find that modal difference vectors identified within LM activations can be used to model fine-grained human categorization behavior. This potentially provides a novel view into how human participants distinguish between modal categories, which we explore by correlating projections along modal difference vectors with human participants' ratings of interpretable features. In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Robust Deep Interpretable Features for Binary Image Classification
papers.research_question: How can we find linearly separated latent representations? What implications on performance do such latent representations have? How can we interpret a model using linearly separated latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Deep Interpretable Features (DIF) framework, which combines deep generative models (IntroVAE) with a supervised objective based on kernel two-sample testing (ME objective) to encourage linear separation in the latent space, leading to more interpretable and robust features for binary image classification.
papers.conclusion: Combining deep generative modeling with a supervised kernel-based two-sample testing objective encourages separation between classes in the latent space, resulting in more interpretable features, improved classification performance with sparse linear models, and increased robustness to adversarial attacks.
papers.key_findings:
DIF achieves better separation in the latent space compared to vanilla IntroVAE and a logistic separation objective, as visualized via UMAP.
DIF improves classification performance with sparser L1-regularized logistic regression models and in some cases outperforms CNN classifiers on test data.
Models trained with DIF exhibit improved robustness to adversarial attacks compared to vanilla models.
DIF isolates interpretable features that correspond to meaningful visual changes (e.g., facial hair, digit width, non-organ matter in lungs).
The imposed linear structure in the latent space leads to smooth latent traversals between classes without artifacts.
papers.limitation: The results presented for the COVID-19 x-ray data are for illustration purposes and further work is needed to draw any medically relevant conclusions based on them.
papers.abstract: The problem of interpretability for binary image classification is considered through the lens of kernel two-sample tests and generative modeling. A feature extraction framework coined Deep Interpretable Features (DIF) is developed, which is used in combination with IntroVAE, a generative model capable of high-resolution image synthesis. Experimental results on a variety of datasets, including COVID-19 chest x-rays demonstrate the benefits of combining deep generative models with the ideas from kernel-based hypothesis testing in moving towards more robust interpretable deep generative models.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Internal Robust Representations for Domain Generalization
papers.research_question: How can consolidating the internal representation of training data improve model generalization under distributional changes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that consolidating the internal representation of training data is a key strategy for improving model generalization in the presence of distributional gaps, with applications in unsupervised domain adaptation and continual learning.
papers.conclusion: Consolidating the internal distribution is a successful approach to improve model generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Consolidating the internal representation of training data improves model generalization under distributional changes.
This strategy can be applied to unsupervised domain adaptation by matching target domain distribution with internal distribution.
In continual learning, maintaining a consolidated internal distribution across tasks mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
papers.abstract: Model generalization under distributional changes remains a significant challenge for machine learning. We present consolidating the internal representation of the training data in a model as a strategy of improving model generalization.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: CoLiDR: Concept Learning using Aggregated Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: How can disentangled generative factors be aggregated into human-understandable concepts to improve interpretability of deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CoLiDR, a method that aggregates disentangled generative factors into human-understandable concepts for interpretable concept-based modeling, achieving parity with state-of-the-art concept-based approaches.
papers.conclusion: CoLiDR unifies disentangled representation learning with concept-based explainability by aggregating generative factors into concepts, providing finer interpretability and maintaining performance.
papers.key_findings:
CoLiDR achieves task accuracy and concept error on par with concept-based models like CBM and GlanceNets.
The method effectively aggregates disentangled generative factors into human-understandable concepts.
Test-time interventions on learned concepts can fix wrongly classified samples, improving debugability.
Visual analysis using GradCAM shows that CoLiDR captures spatial concepts better than CBMs.
CoLiDR is generalizable to arbitrary numbers of concepts and generative factors across different datasets.
future_direction: Utilizing more complex disentanglement architectures like Generative Adversarial Networks.
Exploring causally related concepts instead of independent ones.
papers.abstract: Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks using concept-based models offers a promising way to explain model behavior through human-understandable concepts. A parallel line of research focuses on disentangling the data distribution into its underlying generative factors, in turn explaining the data generation process. While both directions have received extensive attention, little work has been done on explaining concepts in terms of generative factors to unify mathematically disentangled representations and human-understandable concepts as an explanation for downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel method CoLiDR - which utilizes a disentangled representation learning setup for learning mutually independent generative factors and subsequently learns to aggregate the said representations into human-understandable concepts using a novel aggregation/decomposition module. Experiments are conducted on datasets with both known and unknown latent generative factors. Our method successfully aggregates disentangled generative factors into concepts while maintaining parity with state-of-the-art concept-based approaches. Quantitative and visual analysis of the learned aggregation procedure demonstrates the advantages of our work compared to commonly used concept-based models over four challenging datasets. Lastly, our work is generalizable to an arbitrary number of concepts and generative factors - making it flexible enough to be suitable for various types of data.

papers.title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action, combining compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAMS-VAE, a generative model that combines sparsity, compositionality, and disentanglement for perturbation modeling, demonstrating improved predictive performance and interpretability on single-cell sequencing data.
papers.conclusion: SAMS-VAE is a useful model for perturbational screening data, with improved predictive performance and ability to recover factors correlated with biological mechanisms, and may aid in scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAMS-VAE with correlated inference achieves the best test IWELBO and average treatment effect correlation.
SAMS-VAE's latent mask is more predictive of annotated biological pathways than SVAE+.
SAMS-VAE and CPA-VAE perform well on out-of-distribution combinatorial tasks and in low-data settings.
SAMS-VAE improves prediction of nonlinear genetic interactions over a naive linear model.
Correlated inference strategies (correlated zbasal and correlated E) improve model performance.
papers.limitation: The prior on the mask may not enforce sparsity as desired when sample size increases, requiring adjustment of the prior strength to achieve desired sparsity.
future_direction: Studying how perturbations interact and compose in more complex fashion.
Incorporating different forms of prior knowledge into such systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets. In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

papers.title: Supervised Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder for Learning Interpretable Global Representations
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable global representations for each class of data using a supervised approach combined with VQ-VAE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-VQ-VAE, a generative model that integrates supervised learning with VQ-VAE to learn interpretable global representations for each class of data, improving generalization and enabling association discovery between classes.
papers.conclusion: S-VQ-VAE effectively learns interpretable global representations for classes of data, revealing associations between classes and offering benefits for applications like drug development.
papers.key_findings:
S-VQ-VAE achieves lower reconstruction error and higher perplexity than VQ-VAE on MNIST data, indicating better use of embedding codes.
The embedding codes learned by S-VQ-VAE capture class characteristics and reveal similarities between classes, such as between digits 4 and 9 in MNIST.
On LINCS gene expression data, S-VQ-VAE generalizes better with lower test error compared to VQ-VAE.
S-VQ-VAE learns meaningful global representations for perturbagen classes (PCLs), revealing biological associations like between EGFR inhibitors and PDGFR-KIT inhibitors.
The model can be used for data generation and classification, with potential applications in drug development.
future_direction: Extend S-VQ-VAE to semi-supervised scenarios
Extend S-VQ-VAE to multi-labeling data scenarios
papers.abstract: Learning interpretable representations of data remains a central challenge in deep learning. When training a deep generative model, the observed data are often associated with certain categorical labels, and, in parallel with learning to regenerate data and simulate new data, learning an interpretable representation of each class of data is also a process of acquiring knowledge. Here, we present a novel generative model, referred to as the Supervised Vector Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (S-VQ-VAE), which combines the power of supervised and unsupervised learning to obtain a unique, interpretable global representation for each class of data. Compared with conventional generative models, our model has three key advantages: first, it is an integrative model that can simultaneously learn a feature representation for individual data point and a global representation for each class of data; second, the learning of global representations with embedding codes is guided by supervised information, which clearly defines the interpretation of each code; and third, the global representations capture crucial characteristics of different classes, which reveal similarity and differences of statistical structures underlying different groups of data. We evaluated the utility of S-VQ-VAE on a machine learning benchmark dataset, the MNIST dataset, and on gene expression data from the Library of Integrated Network-Based Cellular Signatures (LINCS). We proved that S-VQ-VAE was able to learn the global genetic characteristics of samples perturbed by the same class of perturbagen (PCL), and further revealed the mechanism correlations between PCLs. Such knowledge is crucial for promoting new drug development for complex diseases like cancer.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
