Handling of confounders and unobserved confounding.
Integration of CRL with foundation models like large language models.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) rely on machine learning techniques such as deep learning and generative modeling to achieve state-of-the-art performance across wide-ranging domains. These methods' surprising performance is due in part to their ability to learn implicit "representations" of complex, multi-modal data. Unfortunately, deep neural networks are notoriously black boxes that obscure these representations, making them difficult to interpret or analyze. To resolve these difficulties, one approach is to build new interpretable neural network models from the ground up. This is the goal of the emerging field of causal representation learning (CRL) that uses causality as a vector for building flexible, interpretable, and transferable generative AI. CRL can be seen as a synthesis of three intrinsically statistical ideas: (i) latent variable models such as factor analysis; (ii) causal graphical models with latent variables; and (iii) nonparametric statistics and deep learning. This paper introduces CRL from a statistical perspective, focusing on connections to classical models as well as statistical and causal identifiability results. We also highlights key application areas, implementation strategies, and open statistical questions.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Can RNNs learn Recursive Nested Subject-Verb Agreements?
papers.research_question: Can recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learn recursive nested subject-verb agreements, and how do they represent such structures internally?
papers.core_contribution: RNNs do not learn systematic recursive rules for nested subject-verb agreement but show bounded generalization with primacy and recency effects, and a single unit can encode multiple grammatical numbers.
papers.conclusion: RNNs do not learn systematic recursive rules but approximate nested structures with bounded mechanisms, showing similarities to human cognitive limitations in processing center-embedded sentences.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs generalize to longer subject-verb dependencies but not to deeper tree structures.
LSTM-based models exhibit primacy and recency effects, performing well on outer- and innermost verbs but poorly on middle verbs.
Ablation studies show that a single unit can encode grammatical number for multiple nouns and its ablation dramatically affects performance on outer dependencies.
All tested RNN types, including those with structural bias (ON-LSTM, stack-RNNs, stack-LSTMs), fail to generalize to deeper structures.
Internal dynamics of key units reveal a fractal-like encoding that may implement a memory stack.
future_direction: Explore the similarity between RNN generalization patterns and human cognitive patterns in processing nested structures.
papers.abstract: One of the fundamental principles of contemporary linguistics states that language processing requires the ability to extract recursively nested tree structures. However, it remains unclear whether and how this code could be implemented in neural circuits. Recent advances in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which achieve near-human performance in some language tasks, provide a compelling model to address such questions. Here, we present a new framework to study recursive processing in RNNs, using subject-verb agreement as a probe into the representations of the neural network. We trained six distinct types of RNNs on a simplified probabilistic context-free grammar designed to independently manipulate the length of a sentence and the depth of its syntactic tree. All RNNs generalized to subject-verb dependencies longer than those seen during training. However, none systematically generalized to deeper tree structures, even those with a structural bias towards learning nested tree (i.e., stack-RNNs). In addition, our analyses revealed primacy and recency effects in the generalization patterns of LSTM-based models, showing that these models tend to perform well on the outer- and innermost parts of a center-embedded tree structure, but poorly on its middle levels. Finally, probing the internal states of the model during the processing of sentences with nested tree structures, we found a complex encoding of grammatical agreement information (e.g. grammatical number), in which all the information for multiple words nouns was carried by a single unit. Taken together, these results indicate how neural networks may extract bounded nested tree structures, without learning a systematic recursive rule.

papers.title: Analyzing (In)Abilities of SAEs via Formal Languages
papers.research_question: What are the abilities and inabilities of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in interpreting language models, and how can we make them learn causally relevant features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes SAEs on formal languages, showing that while they can find interpretable features, these features often lack causal impact, and proposes a causal regularization method to incentivize learning of causally relevant features.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causality should be a central target in SAE training, and the proposed method is a proof-of-concept step towards learning causally relevant features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can identify interpretable latents corresponding to grammar features like depth and parts-of-speech.
SAE performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like regularization and normalization.
Interpretable features from standard SAEs do not necessarily have causal effects on model outputs.
The proposed causal regularization method can lead to SAE features with predictable causal impacts.
Top-k regularization outperforms L1 regularization in finding interpretable features.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method is a proof-of-concept and only tested on synthetic formal languages.
The method relies on the availability of correlated tokens for weak supervision, which may not always be present in real-world settings.
future_direction: Overcoming the limitation of relying on correlated tokens
Extending the method to real-world settings
papers.abstract: Autoencoders have been used for finding interpretable and disentangled features underlying neural network representations in both image and text domains. While the efficacy and pitfalls of such methods are well-studied in vision, there is a lack of corresponding results, both qualitative and quantitative, for the text domain. We aim to address this gap by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on a synthetic testbed of formal languages. Specifically, we train SAEs on the hidden representations of models trained on formal languages (Dyck-2, Expr, and English PCFG) under a wide variety of hyperparameter settings, finding interpretable latents often emerge in the features learned by our SAEs. However, similar to vision, we find performance turns out to be highly sensitive to inductive biases of the training pipeline. Moreover, we show latents correlating to certain features of the input do not always induce a causal impact on model's computation. We thus argue that causality has to become a central target in SAE training: learning of causal features should be incentivized from the ground-up. Motivated by this, we propose and perform preliminary investigations for an approach that promotes learning of causally relevant features in our formal language setting.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Integrating Evolutionary and Compositional Features with ML and DL for Robust and Interpretable Druggable Protein Prediction
papers.research_question: How can evolutionary and compositional features be integrated with machine learning and deep learning for robust and interpretable druggable protein prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid feature representation combining Average Block-based PSSM and Dipeptide Composition for druggable protein prediction, achieving high accuracy with statistical validation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid feature representation enables strong predictive performance for druggable protein prediction, with SVM and CapsBiLSTM achieving high accuracy and AUC scores, validated statistically, and providing interpretable insights into sequence descriptors.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid features (AB-PSSM + DPC) significantly outperform individual descriptors in predicting druggable proteins.
SVM and CapsBiLSTM models achieve classification accuracies above 90% and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC scores above 95%.
Statistical tests (DeLong's test, McNemar's test, bootstrap confidence intervals) confirm the robustness and significance of the improvements.
Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: Identification of Knowledge Neurons in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: How can activation-based and integrated gradient-based methods identify knowledge neurons in protein language models to enhance interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that activation-based and integrated gradient-based methods effectively identify knowledge neurons in protein language models, with key neurons in self-attention being particularly important for knowledge expression.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that activation and integrated gradients methods can identify knowledge neurons in protein language models, with key neurons being particularly important, enhancing interpretability for computational biology applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation-based and integrated gradient-based selection methods outperform random selection in identifying knowledge neurons.
Integrated gradients method performs better than activation-based for larger submodels (50% and 25% preserved).
At high sparsity (1% preserved), both methods perform similarly.
Neurons related to key vectors in self-attention are consistently identified as crucial for knowledge expression.
Value vector neurons are less important compared to key and query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in interpreting the specific knowledge each neuron learns
Potential biases in the ESM model due to training data, e.g., overrepresentation of healthy proteins
future_direction: Classifying the types of knowledge encoded by specific neurons beyond binary classification
Extending analysis to different tasks in computational biology
Applying interpretability methods to other protein language models
papers.abstract: Neural language models have become powerful tools for learning complex representations of entities in natural language processing tasks. However, their interpretability remains a significant challenge, particularly in domains like computational biology where trust in model predictions is crucial. In this work, we aim to enhance the interpretability of protein language models, specifically the state-of-the-art ESM model, by identifying and characterizing knowledge neurons - components that express understanding of key information. After fine-tuning the ESM model for the task of enzyme sequence classification, we compare two knowledge neuron selection methods that preserve a subset of neurons from the original model. The two methods, activation-based and integrated gradient-based selection, consistently outperform a random baseline. In particular, these methods show that there is a high density of knowledge neurons in the key vector prediction networks of self-attention modules. Given that key vectors specialize in understanding different features of input sequences, these knowledge neurons could capture knowledge of different enzyme sequence motifs. In the future, the types of knowledge captured by each neuron could be characterized.

papers.title: Efficient Representations are Controllable Representations
papers.research_question: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model’s activations? Can a model's efficiency pressure be exploited to induce interpretable, controllable representations?
papers.core_contribution: By finetuning an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss to write binary feature classifications into a small set of residual stream dimensions, the model reorganizes to depend on these flags, making them genuine internal features that can be used to steer generation at inference time. This works due to the model's efficiency pressure under capacity constraints.
papers.conclusion: The residual stream is writable, and a model's own efficiency pressure can be exploited to induce interpretable and controllable representations. This inverts the usual controllability problem by providing signals that the model will naturally consolidate around.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns to write correct feature flags to the designated 'fenced' dimensions after training.
The model learns to depend on these flags during generation, as shown by overwriting experiments that causally steer generation.
The model erodes its own alternative representations of the fenced features, consolidating feature information into the fenced dimensions.
The efficiency pressure (representational cost) leads the model to consolidate around the reliably supplied feature signals.
The method incurs a negligible perplexity cost when fencing a small number of dimensions, but the cost grows as more dimensions are fenced.
papers.limitation:
Early layers (k < 5) struggle to produce clean flags, consistent with the view that early layers have not yet derived the relevant features.
At the current level of training, the model has begun to erode previous representations but some residual information persists in the remaining dimensions.
papers.abstract: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model's activations? Controlling how LLMs internally represent concepts typically requires sophisticated methods to first identify, then intervene on the model's existing feature geometry. We bypass all of this. We finetune an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss, training 16 of its 3072 residual stream dimensions to be inert interpretability flags that simply indicate what concepts are required for generation. The model reorganizes around them anyway, learning to rely on these flags during actual generation tasks. As a result, these inert flags become genuine internal features: interpretable control switches that allow us to steer generation at inference time. Why does this work? When a feature is reliably supplied at a fixed location, gradient descent gradually eliminates redundant encodings elsewhere, and the model erodes its own alternative representations. A model's efficiency pressure is a lever - exploitable to induce interpretable, controllable representations.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable\n Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: If we know the exact mechanisms under which latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
When the true mechanism is known, the system is identified up to any equivariances of the mechanism.
With multiple known mechanisms, identification is up to equivariances shared by all mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of possible mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises via imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and certain conditions, identification is up to an offset.
The framework generalizes to stochastic mechanisms and can recover existing identifiability results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes the encoder/decoder functions are bijective and that reconstruction is perfectly solved, which is a strong assumption and not easy in practice.
papers.abstract:
A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data
generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that
provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships
between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary
information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the
problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging
knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete
characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge
about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the
exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification
can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying
mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know
some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the
mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based
perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing
identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by
exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of
new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Visual interpretability of image-based classification models by generative latent space disentanglement applied to in vitro fertilization
papers.research_question: How to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models in a human-interpretable way?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a generative model that learns disentangled latent representations to discover and visualize the image properties driving classification decisions, enabling human-interpretable counterfactual explanations.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER enables human-interpretable visual explanations for image classification models, discovers new image properties, and provides transparency for individual predictions, with potential for biological discovery.
papers.key_findings:
DISCOVER successfully identifies known blastocyst quality properties (size and trophectoderm) as classification-driving features.
DISCOVER discovers new properties (blastocoel density) that were not explicitly annotated.
DISCOVER provides instance-specific interpretation, ranking the importance of each property for individual predictions.
DISCOVER generalizes to other domains (natural images and Alzheimer's disease MRI).
DISCOVER outperforms existing interpretability methods (GradCAM, SHAP, LIME) in providing disentangled visual explanations.
papers.limitation:
One latent feature may encode multiple independent semantic image properties (entanglement).
DISCOVER may miss semantic image properties that are associated with the classification task (e.g., inner cell mass was not identified).
The method requires training a generative model, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The success of deep learning in identifying complex patterns exceeding human intuition comes at the cost of interpretability. Non-linear entanglement of image features makes deep learning a "black box" lacking human meaningful explanations for the models' decision. We present DISCOVER, a generative model designed to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models. DISCOVER learns disentangled latent representations, where each latent feature encodes a unique classification-driving visual property. This design enables "human-in-the-loop" interpretation by generating disentangled exaggerated counterfactual explanations. We apply DISCOVER to interpret classification of in vitro fertilization embryo morphology quality. We quantitatively and systematically confirm the interpretation of known embryo properties, discover properties without previous explicit measurements, and quantitatively determine and empirically verify the classification decision of specific embryo instances. We show that DISCOVER provides human-interpretable understanding of "black box" classification models, proposes hypotheses to decipher underlying biomedical mechanisms, and provides transparency for the classification of individual predictions.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Quality of internal representation shapes learning performance in feedback neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the interplay between internal network dynamics and target properties shape learning performance in feedback neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Learning performance in feedback networks is maximized when the target frequency matches a resonance frequency determined by internal connectivity, corresponding to high-dimensional and desynchronized internal representations.
papers.conclusion: The quality of internal representation, shaped by the interplay between network connectivity and target dynamics, is a major determinant of learning success in feedback networks.
papers.key_findings:
Learning performance in feedback networks is non-monotonic with target frequency, with an optimal frequency that decreases with increasing connectivity strength.
The optimal frequency corresponds to a resonance where the internal representation has maximal dimensionality and minimal synchrony.
The condition number of the cross-correlation matrix is minimized at the resonance frequency, making learning more robust.
These findings hold across different training algorithms (LS, ridge, RLS) and for both linear and non-linear networks.
In non-linear networks, the resonance frequency increases with target amplitude.
papers.abstract: The authors find a resonance frequency at which feedback neural networks reproduce a sinusoidal wave, and show that network performance is determined by the robustness of the corresponding internal representation.

papers.title: Steering Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: In this work, we investigate the potential of Activation Steering, a technique originally developed for controlling text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), to direct PLMs toward generating protein sequences with targeted properties.
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first application of activation steering to Protein Language Models, enabling property-specific protein generation without retraining, and proposes a novel optimization framework (ASPO) that integrates activation steering with mutation site identification.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is a viable and powerful paradigm for guiding PLMs to generate and optimize proteins with desired properties, offering a scalable and efficient alternative to traditional methods.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering effectively guides PLMs to generate protein sequences with enhanced thermostability and solubility, outperforming fine-tuning and original models.
The proposed ASPO framework achieves the highest fitness scores in protein optimization tasks for thermostability, solubility, and GFP brightness.
Activation steering maintains or improves sequence diversity and novelty compared to baselines.
The method is sensitive to the size of positive/negative sets and steering strength, with recommended defaults provided.
Activation steering can simultaneously optimize multiple properties.
papers.abstract: Protein Language Models (PLMs), pre-trained on extensive evolutionary data from natural proteins, have emerged as indispensable tools for protein design. While powerful, PLMs often struggle to produce proteins with precisely specified functionalities or properties due to inherent challenges in controlling their outputs. In this work, we investigate the potential of Activation Steering, a technique originally developed for controlling text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), to direct PLMs toward generating protein sequences with targeted properties. We propose a simple yet effective method that employs activation editing to steer PLM outputs, and extend this approach to protein optimization through a novel editing site identification module. Through comprehensive experiments on lysozyme-like sequence generation and optimization, we demonstrate that our methods can be seamlessly integrated into both auto-encoding and autoregressive PLMs without requiring additional training. These results highlight a promising direction for precise protein engineering using foundation models.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders make sense of gene expression latent variable models?
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively used to interpret latent representations in biological data, specifically single-cell gene expression data?
papers.core_contribution: This work explores the potential of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting latent representations in biological data, introduces scFeatureLens for automated annotation of SAE features with biological concepts, and demonstrates that SAEs can extract meaningful features that steer cells into desired biological programs.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that SAEs are a valuable tool for interpreting latent representations in biological data, and the introduced scFeatureLens pipeline provides a scalable framework for improved interpretability in single-cell analysis, though more research is needed in this field.
papers.key_findings:
Distribution type and distance of hidden generative variables affect their recovery from latent representations.
SAEs can extract meaningful features from single-cell expression models that successfully steer cells into desired programs, with features acting either locally or globally.
SAEs can uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed in traditional analysis.
The introduced automated pipeline, scFeatureLens, enables large-scale interpretability analysis by linking SAE features to biological concepts from gene sets.
SAEs do not provide an advantage over simple baselines for recovering known features, but are valuable for discovering unknown features and data generation structure.
papers.limitation:
Variables with an indirect effect on the observed data and little structure in the generative process could practically not be recovered.
SAEs do not pose an advantage in the recovery of known or hypothesized features compared to simple baselines.
The case study was limited to Gene Ontology terms which are incomplete and biased towards well-studied genes.
future_direction: Future work could explore metrics for evaluating the biological meaningfulness in and differences between embeddings.
More research is needed in the field of interpretability for biological models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have lately been used to uncover interpretable latent features in large language models. By projecting dense embeddings into a much higher-dimensional and sparse space, learned features become disentangled and easier to interpret. This work explores the potential of SAEs for decomposing embeddings in complex and high-dimensional biological data. Using simulated data, it outlines the efficacy, hyperparameter landscape, and limitations of SAEs when it comes to extracting ground truth generative variables from latent space. The application to embeddings from pretrained single-cell models shows that SAEs can find and steer key biological processes and even uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed. This work further introduces scFeatureLens, an automated interpretability approach for linking SAE features and biological concepts from gene sets to enable large-scale analysis and hypothesis generation in single-cell gene expression models.

papers.title: Causal Intervention Framework for Variational Auto Encoder Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can causal interventions be used to understand the internal mechanisms of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs, enabling identification of circuit motifs and quantification of interpretability metrics.
papers.conclusion: The causal intervention framework enables detailed understanding of VAE internal mechanisms, with insights into circuit specialization and disentanglement, paving the way for more transparent generative models.
papers.key_findings:
VAEs develop specialized circuit motifs for processing different semantic factors.
FactorVAE achieves higher disentanglement scores and effect strengths compared to standard VAE and β-VAE.
Modularity alone doesn't guarantee disentanglement; causal effect strength is equally important.
Early encoder layers contain polysemantic units, while latent space shows more monosemantic units in FactorVAE.
Causal mediation analysis reveals layer-specific and dimension-specific information flow patterns.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other generative models like diffusion models and GANs
Use insights to design more transparent and controllable generative models
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Mechanistic interpretability of deep learning models has emerged as a crucial research direction for understanding the functioning of neural networks. While significant progress has been made in interpreting discriminative models like transformers, understanding generative models such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) remains challenging. This paper introduces a comprehensive causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs. We develop techniques to identify and analyze "circuit motifs" in VAEs, examining how semantic factors are encoded, processed, and disentangled through the network layers. Our approach uses targeted interventions at different levels: input manipulations, latent space perturbations, activation patching, and causal mediation analysis. We apply our framework to both synthetic datasets with known causal relationships and standard disentanglement benchmarks. Results show that our interventions can successfully isolate functional circuits, map computational graphs to causal graphs of semantic factors, and distinguish between polysemantic and monosemantic units. Furthermore, we introduce metrics for causal effect strength, intervention specificity, and circuit modularity that quantify the interpretability of VAE components. Experimental results demonstrate clear differences between VAE variants, with FactorVAE achieving higher disentanglement scores (0.084) and effect strengths (mean 4.59) compared to standard VAE (0.064, 3.99) and \(\beta\)-VAE (0.051, 3.43). Our framework advances the mechanistic understanding of generative models and provides tools for more transparent and controllable VAE architectures.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: ProtoVAE: A Trustworthy Self-Explainable Prototypical Variational Model
papers.research_question: How to build a self-explainable model that is transparent, diverse, and trustworthy without sacrificing predictive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoV AE, a variational autoencoder-based self-explainable model that learns class-specific prototypes end-to-end, enforces diversity and trustworthiness via regularization, and achieves predictive performance comparable to black-box models.
papers.conclusion: ProtoV AE satisfies the defined properties of transparency, diversity, and trustworthiness for self-explainable models, providing faithful explanations without degrading predictive performance.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoV AE achieves better predictive accuracy than other self-explainable models and matches or exceeds black-box model performance.
The model learns diverse and transparent prototypes that can be visualized in the input space via the decoder.
Local explanation maps generated via Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) are more faithful than those of ProtoPNet.
The orthonormality constraint and VAE loss prevent prototype collapse and ensure intra-class diversity.
ProtoV AE's prototypes represent the 'true mean' of data subsets, providing more flexible and faithful global explanations.
papers.limitation:
The number of prototypes per class is fixed, which may not adapt to classes of varying complexity.
The quality of global explanations (prototype reconstructions) is limited by the decoder's capability.
future_direction: Distance-based pruning of prototypes to adapt their number per class.
Using a prior on the distribution of prototypical similarities to control prototype usage frequency.
Leveraging more expressive generative models (e.g., very deep VAEs, normalizing flows) to improve prototype reconstructions and scalability.
papers.abstract: The need for interpretable models has fostered the development of self-explainable classifiers. Prior approaches are either based on multi-stage optimization schemes, impacting the predictive performance of the model, or produce explanations that are not transparent, trustworthy or do not capture the diversity of the data. To address these shortcomings, we propose ProtoVAE, a variational autoencoder-based framework that learns class-specific prototypes in an end-to-end manner and enforces trustworthiness and diversity by regularizing the representation space and introducing an orthonormality constraint. Finally, the model is designed to be transparent by directly incorporating the prototypes into the decision process. Extensive comparisons with previous self-explainable approaches demonstrate the superiority of ProtoVAE, highlighting its ability to generate trustworthy and diverse explanations, while not degrading predictive performance.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: Learning Causal Representations of Single Cells via Sparse Mechanism Shift Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we learn causal representations of single-cell genomics data by modeling perturbations as interventions on latent variables, leveraging the sparse mechanism shift assumption to improve disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes sVAE+, a Bayesian variant of the sparse VAE for single-cell perturbation data, which models perturbations as stochastic interventions on a sparse subset of latent variables, and demonstrates that it outperforms existing methods in disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: Modeling perturbations as interventions with sparse mechanism shift enables learning causal representations that are more interpretable and generalize better, offering a promising approach for single-cell genomics and perturbation biology.
papers.key_findings:
sVAE+ achieves higher disentanglement scores (MCC) compared to VAE, β-VAE, iVAE, and sVAE on simulated data.
sVAE+ better recovers the causal graph (higher precision, recall, F1) of intervention targets in latent space.
sVAE+ improves out-of-domain generalization, yielding lower interventional negative log-likelihood on held-out perturbations.
On real single-cell perturbation datasets, sVAE+ outperforms other methods in transfer learning tasks.
The sparse mechanism shift assumption is beneficial for learning interpretable causal representations from single-cell perturbation data.
papers.limitation:
The sparsity assumption may be limiting due to indirect downstream effects in biological systems, especially as time passes after the initial perturbation.
The model assumes discrete interventions and may not handle time-resolved measurements without extension.
future_direction: Incorporating time-resolved measurements from single-cell perturbation experiments.
Handling non-sparse interactions and feedback mechanisms in biological pathways.
Extending the noise model to more realistic distributions for scRNA-seq data.
papers.abstract: Latent variable models such as the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) have become a go-to tool for analyzing biological data, especially in the field of single-cell genomics. One remaining challenge is the interpretability of latent variables as biological processes that define a cell's identity. Outside of biological applications, this problem is commonly referred to as learning disentangled representations. Although several disentanglement-promoting variants of the VAE were introduced, and applied to single-cell genomics data, this task has been shown to be infeasible from independent and identically distributed measurements, without additional structure. Instead, recent methods propose to leverage non-stationary data, as well as the sparse mechanism shift assumption in order to learn disentangled representations with a causal semantic. Here, we extend the application of these methodological advances to the analysis of single-cell genomics data with genetic or chemical perturbations. More precisely, we propose a deep generative model of single-cell gene expression data for which each perturbation is treated as a stochastic intervention targeting an unknown, but sparse, subset of latent variables. We benchmark these methods on simulated single-cell data to evaluate their performance at latent units recovery, causal target identification and out-of-domain generalization. Finally, we apply those approaches to two real-world large-scale gene perturbation data sets and find that models that exploit the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis surpass contemporary methods on a transfer learning task. We implement our new model and benchmarks using the scvi-tools library, and release it as open-source software at https://github.com/Genentech/sVAE.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Explaining the Behavior of Black-Box Prediction Algorithms with Causal Learning
papers.research_question: How can we provide causal explanations for black-box prediction models in terms of interpretable macro-level features, especially in the presence of unmeasured confounding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal discovery-based approach (using algorithms like FCI) to explain black-box model predictions in terms of interpretable macro-level features, which can handle unmeasured confounding and distinguish causal features from spurious associations.
papers.conclusion: Causal discovery methods provide a promising approach for explaining black-box models by identifying causal determinants of predictions in terms of interpretable features, advancing towards more trustworthy AI.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies stable causal macro-features for bird classification (e.g., Wing Shape, Wing Pattern) and pneumonia detection (e.g., Atelectasis, Infiltration).
Existing pixel-level explanation methods (LIME, SHAP) are less informative for these tasks as they do not map to interpretable high-level features.
Causal discovery can reveal unmeasured confounding among observed macro-level variables, which is crucial for valid causal explanation.
papers.limitation:
Requires annotated data with interpretable macro-level features, which may not always be available.
Assumes causal sufficiency among the observed variables (though allows unmeasured confounding among them).
Causal discovery algorithms can be computationally expensive and sensitive to statistical errors in independence tests.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other data modalities like text and time series.
Automate the extraction of interpretable features from unannotated data.
Incorporate interventional data when available to improve causal discovery.
papers.abstract: Causal approaches to post-hoc explainability for black-box prediction models (e.g., deep neural networks trained on image pixel data) have become increasingly popular. However, existing approaches have two important shortcomings: (i) the "explanatory units" are micro-level inputs into the relevant prediction model, e.g., image pixels, rather than interpretable macro-level features that are more useful for understanding how to possibly change the algorithm's behavior, and (ii) existing approaches assume there exists no unmeasured confounding between features and target model predictions, which fails to hold when the explanatory units are macro-level variables. Our focus is on the important setting where the analyst has no access to the inner workings of the target prediction algorithm, rather only the ability to query the output of the model in response to a particular input. To provide causal explanations in such a setting, we propose to learn causal graphical representations that allow for arbitrary unmeasured confounding among features. We demonstrate the resulting graph can differentiate between interpretable features that causally influence model predictions versus those that are merely associated with model predictions due to confounding. Our approach is motivated by a counterfactual theory of causal explanation wherein good explanations point to factors that are "difference-makers" in an interventionist sense.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
